passages.title: Conditional whole-space breakdown
passages.quote: Comparison for `Breakdown.breakdown_on_space`: The written profile premise includes extra decay bounds, and the conclusion retains nonexistence for every positive viscosity while omitting the constructed trajectory, rate and convergence in Theorem 1.1. Relating the paper and formal endpoints uses the analytic bridges described in the authors’ README.

comparisons.note: Theorem 1.1 constructs a blow-up trajectory and gives its rate and convergence to the profile. Breakdown.Space.text: The ambient space is ℝ³ with its Euclidean inner product. Every coordinate sum runs over its three standard directions.

Breakdown.unitVector.text: Each coordinate vector has Euclidean norm one. Together they give the standard orthonormal basis used in the differential operators.

Breakdown.divergenceAt.text: The trace gives div v wherever v is differentiable. Smoothness of the solutions and profiles supplies that regularity in the applications.

Breakdown.sumSecondPartialsAt.text: The sum of the three repeated directional second derivatives gives Δv under the stated smoothness assumptions. Writing this expression alone supplies no regularity of v.

Breakdown.gradientAt.text: The three scalar coordinate derivatives reconstruct ∇p. The solution and profile hypotheses supply the pressure regularity needed for this interpretation.

Breakdown.advectionAt.text: The derivative of v applied to v gives (v·∇)v. The regularity needed to interpret it is supplied with the solution or perturbation being considered.

Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution.text: The velocity and pressure are jointly smooth for t≥0, including the initial trace. At positive times the differential equation uses their ordinary time and spatial derivatives.

Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace.text: For each ν>0 the initial datum may be chosen separately. A forbidden global solution may have any finite bound that controls its kinetic energy for every t≥0.

Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus.text: The periodic problem is represented by velocity fields on ℝ³ of period one in each coordinate. The pressure may be any smooth pressure, so the excluded solution class includes pressures without those periods.

Breakdown.SimilarityResidual.text: The time variable is the similarity time s, and the residual is ∂sW+W/2+(y·∇)W/2−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∇q. Its interpretation uses the smoothness of the profile and pressure.

Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.text: The transformation R is orthogonal and may include a reflection. Pointwise nonzero velocity, together with smoothness, rules out changing the zero field only on a null set.

Breakdown.IsTestFunction.text: These are scalar smooth tests with compact spatial support. Time does not enter this test class.

Breakdown.IsWeakGradient.text: The field and its proposed gradient must both be locally integrable. Integration by parts against every scalar smooth compactly supported test identifies the weak gradient.

Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField.text: The test field is smooth and compactly supported jointly in time and space, and has zero spatial divergence. Periodicity is unnecessary for these tests.

Breakdown.weakSimilarityIntegrand.text: Time and transport derivatives fall on the test field, while G supplies the weak spatial gradient of W. Solenoidal tests remove the pressure term.

Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE.text: One finite constant controls both ∫|W(s)|⁶ and the squared operator norm of G at every s. The certificate instead writes the Frobenius norm of the gradient, which is equivalent in dimension three.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_space.text: Existence of a nonzero recurrent profile is the hypothesis of the implication. Producing or validating a numerical certificate is a separate step.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus.text: The conclusion excludes global smooth periodic velocities without giving a blow-up time, rate or profile-convergence estimate. The readable statement presents the implication and refers to a separate proof.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_space_of_weak.text: The weak residual must be integrable, and the velocity must be nonzero as a space-time almost-everywhere class. Changing the zero field at isolated points cannot meet these requirements.

Breakdown.Symmetry.text: A symmetry consists of an orthogonal spatial transformation and a shift $\theta_0$ in normalized time. In similarity time the shift becomes $\theta_0S$, as in (7.39).

Breakdown.matSq.text: The squared norm is $\sum_j|G(e_j)|^2$. With $G(e_j)_k=\partial_jv_k$, this is exactly the Frobenius square $|\nabla v|^2$ used in the paper.

Breakdown.matInner.text: The pairing is $\sum_jG(e_j)\cdot K(e_j)$. Matching the derivative direction $j$ and vector component $k$ gives the paper's Frobenius matrix pairing.

Breakdown.secondDerivTrace.text: The expression is $\sum_jH(e_j,e_j)$. Its identification with $\Delta v$ uses the separate requirement that $H$ is the weak Hessian of $v$.

Breakdown.periodLIntegral.text: The formula integrates max(f,0) over [0,1]×ℝ³ and may have value ∞. It agrees with the intended integral for nonnegative densities; converting it to a finite real value requires a finiteness proof.

Breakdown.periodBallLIntegral.text: The spatial integral is restricted to the closed ball of radius r. A nonpositive r gives a null domain, and the nonnegative density integral can still be infinite for positive r.

Breakdown.periodNorm.text: For measurable F with finite squared integral this is ∥F∥H. Outside that class the formula assigns zero to an infinite squared integral, so the finiteness assumptions in the estimates are essential.

Breakdown.periodBallNorm.text: Global square integrability makes the ball-restricted squared integral finite. The radius may be nonpositive, in which case this local contribution vanishes.

Breakdown.vecNorm.text: This is the ordinary Euclidean norm of the finite coefficient vector. In dimension zero the sole vector is zero and its norm is zero, as permitted in §7.

Breakdown.IsTimePeriodic.text: The recurrence f(θ+1,y)=f(θ,y) holds pointwise for every θ and y. It is stated even when other properties of f concern almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestVector.text: These vector tests have compact support jointly in time and space. Their divergence is unrestricted, and no time period is imposed.

Breakdown.IsPerturbation.text: The supplied field $g$ represents $S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+v/2+(y\cdot\nabla)v/2$ and belongs to $H$. Positivity of $S$ comes from the certificate, while $\Delta v$ is supplied separately through the Hessian trace.

Breakdown.IsRightSide.text: The weak equation pairs F with every solenoidal space-time test. Measurability and finite H norm of F are additional hypotheses in the coercive estimate, and diffusion enters through the gradient pairing.

Breakdown.weightedEnergy.text: For the positive bounded measurable weight and admissible derivatives, the expression is ∥v∥w² from (7.14). These hypotheses ensure a nonnegative finite density integral before it is represented by a real number.

Breakdown.pinValue.text: The pin is the period pairing of ∇v with Ξᵢ. Square integrability of both matrix fields makes the pairing integrable; Ξᵢ need not itself be a derivative in this definition.

Breakdown.IsProfileField.text: The stationary test belongs to L⁶(ℝ³), has an L² weak gradient and an L² Laplacian. Only symmetries with zero time shift constrain it.

Breakdown.frozenForm.text: The test velocity is paired with the linearized convection terms and −Δu. The other contributions are ∥Δu∥₂² and one quarter of ∥∇u∥₂², as in (7.22).

Breakdown.stationaryEnergy.text: With G=∇u and tr H=Δu, this is ∫(|Δu|²+w|∇u|²). Its integral interpretation uses the positive bounded weight and the stationary test's square integrability.

Breakdown.defectField.text: The earlier certificate chooses a residual using a C¹ scalar pressure. Its reciprocal period factor has the intended time-scaling meaning when the certificate supplies S>0.

Breakdown.supBoundFactor.text: For $w^*>0$ the constant is $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w^*})^{-1/2}$. Positivity of $w^*$ is supplied by the certificate.

Breakdown.CertificateData.text: These are proposed values; their signs, regularity and bounds are imposed by separate certificate conditions. This earlier formulation uses unit force weight and coercivity at the approximate profile itself.

Breakdown.CertificateData.box.text: Every coordinate lies between its centre minus its radius and its centre plus its radius. Nonnegative radii place the centre in the box, including in dimension zero.

Breakdown.IsCertificate.text: The coercive estimate covers every admissible perturbation and every measurable periodic square-integrable right-hand side. Joint C² regularity of the approximate family and decay of its second derivative are additional written requirements relative to §7.2.

Breakdown.CertificateHypothesis.text: The hypothesis asks for a finite dimension and data satisfying every earlier certificate condition. The dimension may be zero, but the remaining analytic conditions still apply.

Breakdown.certificate_orbit.text: The conclusion asserts existence of a weak recurrent profile. It omits the selected parameter, exact selected period, prescribed symmetry family and quantitative correction bounds retained in Theorem 7.1.

Breakdown.CoerciveClause.text: The estimate is uniform over parameters, perturbations, coefficient vectors and admissible right-hand sides. Its local term is an L² norm on a ball, whereas (7.17) uses finitely many directional pairings.

Breakdown.periodPairing.text: The H pairing is interpreted as an iterated space and period integral. Measurability and finite squared integrals justify its integrability in the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate.

Breakdown.MultiplierInequality.text: The multiplier and nonnegative frequency size may depend on the perturbation and its right-hand side. This earlier inequality uses a ball-restricted forcing norm and unit weight on the force coefficients.

Breakdown.periodPairing_abs_le.text: Both fields must be measurable up to a null set and have finite squared period integrals. These assumptions give an integrable pairing and the usual Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

Breakdown.coercive_scalar_core.text: The assumptions include $c>0$, nonnegative energy and squared coefficient size, and nonnegative retained frequency coefficient. The resulting coefficients are $a/\sqrt{c}$, $K$ and $\sqrt{t/c}$.

Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_multiplierIn.text: The three resulting coefficients may be enlarged because their corresponding norms are nonnegative. The period Cauchy–Schwarz inequality supplies the required pairing bound.

Breakdown.axialRot.text: This is the ordinary rotation about the third spatial axis. The coordinate labels 0,1,2 correspond to the paper's first, second and third coordinates.

Breakdown.modeAverage.text: Time is integrated over a unit interval and angle over an interval of length 2π. The factor 1/(2π) and the conjugate exponential give the stated Fourier normalization.

Breakdown.modeVel.text: The direct frequencies are (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁). Rotating the argument forward and the vector backward gives the rotating-frame mode in (B.12).

Breakdown.modeGrad.text: The first matrix index is the vector component and the second is the derivative direction. The weak-gradient relation between G and v is imposed with the perturbation.

Breakdown.modeSecondDeriv.text: The three indices are the vector component and the two derivative directions. Weak-derivative compatibility is imposed separately, and the mode amplitude uses the sum of squared component moduli.

Breakdown.cnormSq.text: The squared modulus is summed over all components of the vector, matrix or tensor. For matrices and tensors this is the Frobenius norm; the scalar conversion-weight Hessians instead use operator norms.

Breakdown.curlOfGrad.text: The entry indexed by (l,j) represents ∂ⱼvₗ. Contracting it with the alternating symbol gives the usual curl orientation.

Breakdown.curlGradOfSecondDeriv.text: This contraction gives the gradient of curl when H is the weak Hessian. Compatibility and almost-everywhere symmetry of the derivatives come from the perturbation assumptions.

Breakdown.cylRadius.text: The cylindrical radius is $\sqrt{y_1^2+y_2^2}$ and vanishes on the rotation axis. The angular-gain inequalities hold almost everywhere, allowing that null axis to be excluded.

Breakdown.IsAxisymmetric.text: The scalar coefficient is unchanged at every point under every axial rotation. The requirement is pointwise.

Breakdown.shiftedFrequency.text: The frequency is 2πn/S+kν(y), with S>0 supplied by admissibility. Here k is already the azimuthal frequency κι₁ of the paper.

Breakdown.meanField.text: The zero time-angle mode is reconstructed as a real vector by taking its real components. Evaluating that mode at time zero still includes averaging over the full period.

Breakdown.curlVec.text: Applying the alternating-symbol contraction to a derivative matrix gives its curl vector. The matrix must represent the field's derivative for this terminology to have its analytic meaning.

Breakdown.vortGrad.text: The Hessian is contracted to give ∂m(curl W)ⱼ. Its relation to derivatives of W is supplied by the regularity or weak-Hessian assumptions.

Breakdown.stretchForm.text: The classical stretching expression uses first and second derivatives of a C² reference field. The active certificate replaces the latter by a specified weak Hessian.

Breakdown.FlowBounds.text: The proposed majorants acquire their meaning through pointwise bounds tied to the same reference profile. Merely listing their numerical values establishes no inequality.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.text: The class assignment covers every integer frequency pair, so at least one class exists. Finiteness, parity, signs, decay and denominator bounds are imposed separately.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.eps.text: The absolute value is used for the nonnegative curl-weight magnitude. The signed weight is retained in the multiplier pairing.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.mu.text: The velocity-weight magnitude is an absolute value and is therefore nonnegative. Its admissibility conditions impose the additional analytic bounds.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.dop.text: The shifted frequency uses the rotation rate of the mode's class. Its intended time-scaling interpretation uses the separately required positive period.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsGrad.text: Admissible weights are Lipschitz and hence differentiable almost everywhere. A value assigned to the derivative at an exceptional point supplies no additional regularity there.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.muGrad.text: The derivative norm is used with the weight's Lipschitz and decay conditions. Those conditions supply its almost-everywhere analytic interpretation.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsNb.text: The maximum is over the finite list of neighboring reference harmonics. It equals zero when that list is empty.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.muNb.text: The finite maximum measures velocity weights at neighboring modes. An empty reference-wave list contributes zero.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.ind.text: The indicator is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. It serves a mathematical definition of the coefficient formulas, without asserting that membership can be decided by a finite computation.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.shareHat.text: The first share is charged when the curl weight or its derivative is active, and the second when a neighboring curl weight is active. The conversion coefficient D must fit below the remaining share.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.secondDerivNorm.text: This is the operator norm of the scalar weight's second derivative. C² regularity of D and Z is required before their Hessians enter the estimates.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefA.text: The error shares in the denominators are controlled by admissibility. This coefficient belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier and includes its transport and reference-wave losses.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefAA.text: The gradient coefficient can have either sign. Nonnegativity of the complete mode density is a further lower-bound problem.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.penalty.text: A weight that is nonzero somewhere can activate a penalty at a point where it vanishes. The Young parameters in the denominators have positive lower bounds.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefB.text: The velocity coefficient can be negative. Its sign is handled by the subsequent density lower bounds.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefC.text: The coefficient multiplies the gradient-velocity product with a minus sign in the assembled density. This mixed product is part of the earlier class-based estimate.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeDensity.text: The five amplitudes are ordered as Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity. The scalar formula also includes a mixed gradient-velocity term and does not itself assert that its inputs arise from a field.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeTerm.text: Each inserted amplitude is the square root of a finite sum of squared complex moduli. The perturbation conditions identify G and H with the weak derivatives of v.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.frequencySeminormS.text: The nonnegative sum and integral retain ∞ when the frequency energy diverges. The multiplier theorem proves finiteness before this energy is used as an ordinary real norm.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsAdmissible.text: Lipschitz regularity supplies almost-everywhere derivatives of the signed weights. The first share may vanish only where both its curl weight and derivative are inactive, and the other displayed denominators have positive guards.

Breakdown.gradField.text: This is the spatial derivative of W where W is differentiable. C² regularity in the classical multiplier theorem supplies the needed regularity.

Breakdown.secondDerivField.text: The iterated derivative supplies the classical Hessian in the C² route. The weak route instead specifies a Hessian and verifies its distributional derivative identities.

Breakdown.symPartForm.text: For real vectors u, the scalar u·Gu equals u·((G+Gᵀ)/2)u. The antisymmetric part contributes zero.

Breakdown.FlowBounds.IsValid.text: Each proposed majorant is tied to W by an inequality, and the harmonic reconstruction holds at every time and point. The finite list is therefore checked against the actual reference field.

Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestField.text: Each test has one support radius that works for every time. It is smooth, period one and pointwise divergence-free.

Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestPotential.text: Each scalar test potential is smooth and period one, with a single spatial support radius. Orthogonality of the multiplier to their gradients expresses its divergence-free condition.

Breakdown.cdot.text: The complex pairing is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second. This convention is retained in the Fourier multiplier identity.

Breakdown.cdotMat.text: The matrix pairing sums the products with the conjugates of the second matrix's nine components. It is the complex Frobenius pairing.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: The Fourier pairing identity uses an infinite real series whose convergence is proved under admissibility. Finite multiplier norm and compactly supported smooth tests give integrable pressure-orthogonality pairings.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityPos.text: The positive part is taken separately for each complete mode term and for J, then summed. The result may be ∞.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityNeg.text: The negative mode masses and the negative part of J are summed without cancellation. Their total finiteness is required by the later assembly argument.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierConstant.text: The constant uses the three bounds nλ, n∇λ and nμ and positive c,cμ,w∗. Setting c=3/50 gives the printed factor 50/3 in the squared multiplier bound.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierGap.text: The frequency energy is represented by a real number only after the multiplier theorem proves it finite. The same multiplier appears in the residual and forcing-field pairings.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplier_density.text: This earlier multiplier theorem assumes a C² reference field and class-based signed weights. The readable implication is proved separately, and the active certificate uses the later weak-Hessian piece formulation.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.azimuthalDensity_n.text: The two angular-gain inequalities are explicit hypotheses of this scalar lemma. Their analytic justification applies almost everywhere away from the rotation axis.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.mode_azimuthal_gai.text: The two bounds hold almost everywhere in space-time and assume |k|≥2. The other two curl-related inequalities in (B.35) are outside this particular conclusion.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretchCharge.text: The factor $\sqrt{2}+1/2$ belongs to the earlier mean-and-wave stretching estimate. Its balancing length is required to be positive in the theorem using the bound.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretch_mean_bound.text: The left side is the positive part of minus the time-angle mean of J. The inequality holds almost everywhere in space and permits an infinite nonnegative series on its right.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.le_of_ennreal_boun.text: Finite negative mass is essential: taking both masses to be ∞ would make the premises hold even for X=0 and Y=1. The proof first obtains finite positive mass, then cancels the signed contributions.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierInequali.text: The additional density bound must hold for every multiplier compatible with the perturbation. Its finite negative mass allows it to be combined with the multiplier existence theorem.

Breakdown.EpsPiece.text: The mode set may be infinite and is unrestricted at the data stage. The positive one-sided frequency condition later makes it disjoint from its negative.

Breakdown.MuPiece.text: A piece may contain infinitely many modes even though only finitely many pieces are used. An empty piece family removes that contribution and leaves the other certificate requirements in force.

Breakdown.HarmonicBounds.text: The mode bounds and the bounds for full vorticity are proposed majorants until the admissibility inequalities are supplied. The full vorticity-gradient bound uses an operator norm.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.text: The curl and velocity piece families are finite, while individual mode sets may be infinite. Signs, regularity and bounds are imposed by admissibility.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.sgn.text: If a mode belongs both to a set and its negative, the definition assigns the positive sign first. Oddness holds under the one-sided frequency condition that excludes this overlap.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.inPiece.text: Membership tests the union of a mode set with its negative. The multiplier sign is specified separately.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.fwdSum.text: Only the finite reference-harmonic list is summed, even when the piece mode set is infinite. The amplitude bound belongs to the shifting reference harmonic.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.backSum.text: The sum includes a reference harmonic when subtracting it exits the selected mode set. Membership of the starting mode is tested separately when this sum is used.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.inward.text: For an overlapping set the positive representative is chosen first. Admissibility excludes that overlap by its one-sided frequency condition.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.outward.text: The positive and negative representatives are tested separately. Both can contribute when neither belongs to the selected mode set.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.harmonicSum.text: The finite reference-harmonic list includes zero under admissibility. The earlier oscillatory-wave list excludes zero and treats the mean separately.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq.text: The rotation rate is a scalar for the fixed piece and parameter. The frequency 2πn/S+kνp is used with S>0.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.wtGrad.text: Lipschitz regularity gives almost-everywhere derivatives of the piece weights. Values assigned at nondifferentiable spline knots add no smoothness claim.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.shareHat.text: The first share is active if either the weight or its derivative contributes, and the outward share is active for positive weight. The balancing scale is positive under admissibility.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefA.text: Different pieces contribute additively even when their mode sets overlap. Each piece has positive allocation parameters, lengths and scales under the admissibility conditions.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefAA.text: The Hessian loss uses the operator norm of the scalar conversion weight D. The perturbation's tensor amplitudes use their componentwise Euclidean norms.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefB.text: Every velocity-piece Young parameter ηp is positive under admissibility. The complete coefficient I₀ still requires the later lower-bound analysis.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeDensity.text: The arguments are Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity amplitudes. Admissibility ensures I′₂≥0; the other coefficients enter the subsequent region and cell estimates.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm.text: The five inserted amplitudes are nonnegative by construction. Their derivative interpretation uses the perturbation's weak-gradient and weak-Hessian conditions.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.seminormSq.text: Nonnegative velocity weights make the density the intended frequency energy. Its extended nonnegative value may be ∞ until the multiplier theorem proves finiteness.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: The infinite Fourier pairing series is proved convergent for admissible inputs. Each test is periodic in time and has a common compact spatial support.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityPos.text: Positive parts are taken separately for each complete mode density and for J. Summation preserves ∞ without subtracting a negative mass.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityNeg.text: The negative density retains an infinite mass if one occurs. A finite-negative-mass result is needed before using the difference of positive and negative integrals.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierGap.text: The multiplier theorem proves the frequency energy finite before real conversion. Keeping the same multiplier in all pairings permits the forcing-field terms to cancel.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsAdmissible.text: Each piece has one strictly positive lower frequency bound for all its modes. Oddness of the frame frequency then excludes zero and overlap with the negative mode set.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.piece_multiplier_.text: The classical theorem assumes a C² reference profile. The active certificate instead uses the weak-Hessian extension, which allows a C¹ profile with the specified weak second derivative.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierInequal.text: The remainder-density hypothesis is uniform over every compatible multiplier and includes finite negative mass. The proof applies it to the same multiplier selected by the multiplier theorem.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text: For nonnegative weights and square-integrable rows, the formula is √(∑aτa⟨F,ea⟩H²). Orthonormal unit rows with these weights reproduce the paper's weighted orthogonal rows.

Breakdown.weakDefectField.text: The C¹ profile assumptions justify the time derivative and first spatial derivative. The separately specified Hessian is linked to the gradient by its weak derivative identities.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.text: The parameter variable here represents α in the paper and is independent of the pressure q. Positivity, invertibility, regularity and bounds are conditions on the proposed data.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params.text: The complementary constraint uses ϱ∗²; the certificate also requires ϱ∗≥0 and nonzero coordinate scales. Dimension zero leaves one parameter vector, so the analytic requirements remain meaningful.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows.text: The chosen rows must be square integrable and their weights nonnegative for the usual seminorm interpretation. These properties are supplied with the full certificate.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect.text: The residual is bounded separately at each parameter. Continuity of the residual as an H-valued function of α is not required.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target.text: The prescribed correction pin is the total target minus the pin of the approximate profile. This difference is the paper's ℓ̄(α).

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjust.text: The index j selects a column of V, so the transformed force vector is Vᵀβ. The adjoint fields and their pin-coupling matrix need no parameter continuity for these estimates.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat.text: The discrepancy is the vector of forcing-field pairings with ψα,j minus the column Vj. Square-integrability assumptions give these pairings their H-inner-product meaning.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.text: The full certificate includes the signs, regularity and finite integrals needed by every formula. Its joint global C¹ parameter dependence and pointwise decaying weak Hessian are additional written requirements relative to §7.2.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateHypothesis.text: This names the existence of data satisfying every extended certificate condition. Establishing it still requires the data and verification of their inequalities.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.withUn.text: For positive ω the force fields and coefficients are rescaled reciprocally, preserving their product. The preservation theorem obtains ω>0 from the certificate.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.atProf.text: The reference error is absorbed using ϑ<1. Consequently all rescalings by 1−ϑ use a positive denominator.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit.text: The formal premise includes additional representative and regularity conditions. The conclusion asserts weak-profile existence and omits the selected parameter, precise period, all prescribed symmetries and quantitative bounds of Theorem 7.1.

Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivSq.text: This is the Frobenius square of the full Hessian. Equality of its integrated energy with the Laplacian energy is an analytic identity, rather than a pointwise equality of these expressions.

Breakdown.Coercive.baseDensity.text: The arguments represent Hessian, gradient of curl, gradient, curl and velocity amplitudes. The Hessians of D and Z have their ordinary meaning under the C² conversion-weight assumptions.

Breakdown.Coercive.velAmp.text: The velocity-mode amplitude is the Euclidean norm of its three complex components. The Fourier integral has its intended meaning under the field's integrability assumptions.

Breakdown.Coercive.gradAmp.text: The gradient-mode amplitude is the Frobenius norm of its nine complex components. The Fourier integral and gradient interpretation use the perturbation assumptions.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortAmp.text: The curl-mode amplitude is the Euclidean norm after contracting the gradient mode. The Fourier integrals use the perturbation's integrability assumptions.

Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivAmp.text: The Hessian-mode amplitude sums the squared moduli of all its components before taking a square root. Its identification with the second derivative mode uses the weak-Hessian conditions.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradAmp.text: The gradient-of-curl amplitude is the Frobenius norm of the corresponding contraction of the Hessian mode. The underlying Fourier integrals use the admissibility assumptions.

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSplitLowerBound.text: The first requirement makes the negative mode remainders and block errors integrable. Finiteness of the entire negative density, including J, is established separately.

Breakdown.Coercive.edgeSum.text: The one-sided frequency bound makes a piece disjoint from its negative. The interactions are summed over the finite reference-harmonic list whose coverage is checked separately.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceNorm.text: The expression has its ℓ² meaning when the mode amplitudes are square summable. Fourier square-sum estimates supply this fact where the expression is used.

Breakdown.Coercive.frameSpeedSup.text: The time-angle supremum has its usual real-valued meaning when the transport speed has a finite upper bound. The pointwise admissibility bounds supply that majorant.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortSup.text: The vorticity majorant bounds the norm at every time and angle. This gives the finite bound required for the real supremum.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradSup.text: The classical vorticity-gradient expression uses C² regularity of the reference field. Its admissibility bound supplies a finite majorant for the time-angle supremum.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsPos.text: For admissible data λp≥0, and the selected frequencies have a positive one-sided lower bound. Thus this contribution to the squared curl amplitude is nonnegative.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsBlock.text: Fourier square summability and pointwise boundedness justify the real mode-set norms and suprema. They are the analytic conditions behind this block expression.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuPos.text: Admissibility supplies 0<cμ<1 and μp≥0. Hence the retained velocity-frequency gain is nonnegative.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuRestMode.text: The Young parameter ηp is positive by admissibility. This is the condition needed for the reciprocal coefficient in the interaction estimate.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuBlock.text: The mode-set square sums have their norm interpretation through the Fourier summability estimates. The formula collects transport and frame-rotation losses for one velocity piece.

Breakdown.Coercive.piecePos.text: Both piece families are finite and may be empty. The base mode density is kept separately from this sum of frequency gains.

Breakdown.Coercive.transportPart.text: The combined field is $g=S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+v/2+(y\cdot\nabla)v/2=T_sv+\Delta v$. For weak perturbations its meaning is imposed through integration by parts.

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothPerturbation.text: The velocity has L⁶ spatial slices and a weighted L² bound over one period. Unweighted L² velocity and the prescribed Γ symmetries are not requirements of this approximation class.

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothApproximation.text: The four nonnegative squared-error integrals tend to zero, so their convergence retains the relevant finiteness information. The approximating fields need no Γ-invariance condition of their own.

Breakdown.Coercive.SmoothApproximationHo.text: This names the assertion that every admissible weak perturbation has the specified smooth approximation. Its proof is provided separately in the analytic development.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv.text: At each time, every first spatial derivative has the specified weak derivative. The Hessian also satisfies a pointwise inverse-cubic decay bound.
For every fixed time the Hessian is symmetric in its two derivative directions almost everywhere in space. The exceptional spatial null set may depend on time.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap.text: The contraction becomes ∇curl W when its tensor is the Hessian of a C² field. That identification is established by the separate derivative identity.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith.text: The weak-Hessian conditions identify the supplied tensor with the second spatial derivative of W. With that identification the contraction gives J in (B.18).

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap_secon.text: The identity explicitly assumes C² regularity of W. It identifies the Hessian contraction with the ordinary spatial derivative of curl W.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityPosWith.text: The positive part is taken after each complete mode density is formed, then summed with the positive part of J. An infinite total remains ∞.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith.text: The negative part of a real quantity a is max(−a,0). The formula sums these masses separately and introduces no cancellation of infinities.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak.text: The harmonic bounds alone do not identify the proposed Hessian with derivatives of W. The multiplier theorem also assumes that weak-derivative link, and allows any c∈(0,1) before the specialization c=3/50.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.isAdmissibleWeak_.text: The conversion uses the identity between the Hessian contraction and ∇curl W for C² fields. The library states that identity separately and supplies its proof before applying the conversion.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe.text: Positive and negative density masses are retained separately. The later remainder estimate supplies finite negative mass, while the multiplier assertion already requires finite frequency energy.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: This is a conditional analytic multiplier theorem. The remaining density lower bound and verification of the numerical certificate are separate obligations.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith.text: The weak-Hessian majorant supplies boundedness for the real time-angle supremum. A separate weak-derivative condition links the tensor to the reference field.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith_s.text: The equality of suprema uses the identity between the Hessian contraction and ∇curl W for C² fields. The library proves that identity separately before the conversion.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsBlockWith.text: Fourier summability and the pointwise profile majorants justify the mode-set norms and suprema. The supplied weak Hessian contributes through the vorticity-gradient bound.
The classical block formula is recovered from the weak-Hessian formula for C² fields. The conversion uses the separately proved identity for the derivative of curl W.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceBlockWith_se.text: The block conversion is applied throughout the finite family of curl pieces. C² regularity supplies the derivative-of-curl identity needed to recover the classical supremum.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceFieldExistsW.text: This assertion concerns multiplier existence and its norm, before use of the residual equation or forcing fields. The extra decay parameter has no hypothesis attached to it in this statement.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceDensityPassa.text: A convergent smooth approximating sequence is an explicit hypothesis of the passage step. The conclusion keeps positive and negative contributions separate.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceAbsorbStepWe.text: Admissibility and the linked weak Hessian supply the positive allocation parameters and analytic bounds. The assertion describes absorption of the error products and does not validate a numerical choice of coefficients.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: The implication assumes multiplier existence, smooth approximation, passage to the limit and absorption of errors. Their separate proofs yield the complete multiplier result.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.ExtendedCoerciveC.text: The right-hand side F may have a gradient component. It is required to be measurable, period one and square integrable before its H norm and row seminorm enter the estimate.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rows_nonneg.text: The square-root expression is always nonnegative, including when its argument is negative. Its seminorm interpretation additionally requires nonnegative row weights and integrable pairings.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.zero_mem_params.text: The origin satisfies the mixed constraint as soon as the coordinate radii on J are nonnegative. Because the complementary radius is squared, this particular conclusion needs neither its sign nor nonzero scales.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowMultiplierIneq.text: The general coefficients c and t specialize to 3/50 and 1000 in the paper. The auxiliary n is a nonnegative frequency size, independent of the parameter-space dimension.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause.text: The remainder bound covers every admissible perturbation, residual and compatible multiplier. It includes finite negative density and allows general c and t before their printed specialization.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq.text: The origin belongs to the parameter set, so parameterwise admissibility supplies positivity of the common coefficients c and cμ. Finite negative mass makes the combination of the density bounds valid.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: The implication still assumes admissibility, a linked reference Hessian, the remainder-density inequality and the two scalar coefficient comparisons. It therefore converts verified inputs to coercivity without itself validating a numerical certificate.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_space.text: Theorem 1.1 constructs a blow-up trajectory and gives its rate and convergence to the profile. The formal implication instead concludes nonexistence of a global finite-energy smooth solution for each positive viscosity, and its profile hypothesis explicitly adds second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus.text: Theorem 1.1 gives a periodic blow-up trajectory, rate and local profile-convergence estimate. The formal implication omits those quantitative conclusions, adds written profile-decay conditions and excludes global periodic velocities even when the pressure is not assumed periodic.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_space_of_weak.text: The paper passes from the weak profile through the regularity result of Proposition 7.11 and then applies Theorem 1.1. The formal implication states the combined route from an explicit weak-profile hypothesis directly to whole-space nonexistence.

Breakdown.certificate_orbit.text: Theorem 7.1 uses the finite-row seminorm and mixed box-and-ellipsoid parameter set with adjoint estimates. This formal implication starts from the earlier box-and-local-ball certificate and concludes weak-profile existence without retaining the selected parameter and quantitative bounds.

Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_isCertificat.text: The paper assumes the a priori estimate as part of a certificate. This formal statement extracts the already assumed estimate from the earlier certificate, retaining its ball-restricted norm and unit force weight.

Breakdown.periodPairing_abs_le.text: Lemma B.2 uses Cauchy–Schwarz for fields in the periodic space H. The formal estimate applies on [0,1]×ℝ³ to all measurable square-integrable fields, so it also covers fields without time periodicity.

Breakdown.le_add_of_sq_le.text: Lemma B.2 uses P²≤aP+Q² to obtain P≤a+Q for nonnegative quantities. The formal scalar implication is the same after identifying x with P and b with Q.

Breakdown.coercive_scalar_core.text: Lemma B.2 uses the printed coefficients $c=3/50$ and $t=1000$. The formal scalar argument allows arbitrary coefficients satisfying the displayed signs and gives the corresponding factors $a/\sqrt{c}$ and $\sqrt{t/c}$.

Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_multiplierIn.text: Lemma B.2 converts the multiplier and density bounds into an a priori estimate with finite rows and a weighted force vector. The formal target here is the earlier estimate with a local-ball term and unit force weight.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplier_density.text: Proposition B.1 uses finite families of multiplier pieces and a reference field with a weak Hessian. This earlier formal theorem uses signed class weights, a mixed gradient-velocity density term and a C² reference field.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.diagonalDensity_no.text: The paper uses scalar positivity within its pointwise region tests. The formal statement isolates the sufficient conditions θ≥0, A≥0, B≥0 and C²≤4AB for a quadratic form with one mixed term.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.azimuthalDensity_n.text: Lemma B.5 establishes angular estimates and treats the five-coefficient density. The formal scalar lemma assumes two angular-gain inequalities and uses them to prove positivity of a reduced form with one mixed term.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.mode_azimuthal_gai.text: Equation (B.35) contains four angular and curl inequalities. The formal statement retains the velocity-to-gradient and gradient-to-Hessian gains under |k|≥2, so its conclusion covers only those two estimates.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretch_mean_bound.text: The paper's cell estimate uses its cell-specific coefficient bounds. The formal statement is the earlier time-angle mean bound for J, with the separate mean-and-wave majorants and its own constants.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.le_of_ennreal_boun.text: Lemma B.2 combines finite signed density integrals. The formal scalar statement spells out that cancellation using two inequalities between nonnegative masses, with finite negative mass as an explicit hypothesis.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierInequali.text: Lemma B.2 combines the piecewise multiplier and finite-row density estimates. This formal implication performs the corresponding cancellation for the earlier class-based multiplier and ball-restricted forcing norm.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.piece_multiplier_.text: Proposition B.1 is used for a C¹ reference field with a specified weak Hessian and c=3/50. This classical formal theorem uses the same five-term piece density, assumes C² regularity and permits general c.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierInequal.text: The paper combines piecewise multiplier bounds with finite residual rows and the weighted force norm. This formal implication uses the piecewise multiplier but concludes the earlier estimate with a ball-restricted term and unit force weight.

Breakdown.isExtendedCertificate_withUnit.text: The paper introduces the positive force weight ω in (7.14). The formal statement shows that reciprocally rescaling force fields and coefficients to set ω=1 preserves every certificate condition.

Breakdown.isExtendedCertificate_atProfil.text: After (7.21), the paper explains absorption of the reference-profile error when ϑ<1. The formal statement asserts that the resulting rescaling preserves the complete certificate, including rows, pins and residual allowances.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit.text: Theorem 7.1 retains a selected α, its period, the prescribed symmetries and the bounds (7.38). The formal implication adds explicit representative and regularity hypotheses and concludes existence of a weak profile without retaining all that same-profile information.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.isWeakSecondDeriv.text: Section 7 supplies a parameter family of approximate profiles. The formal statement fixes an admissible parameter and gathers its C¹ regularity, periodicity, divergence and weak-Hessian conditions for the multiplier argument.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv.text: The paper uses the symmetry of weak second derivatives in its multiplier calculus. The formal statement makes the quantifiers explicit: at each fixed time the Hessian is symmetric almost everywhere in space.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith_s.text: The paper writes one stretching expression J in (B.18). The formal identity states that supplying the classical Hessian in the weak-Hessian formula gives that same expression.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap_secon.text: The paper writes ∇curl W directly. Under C² regularity the formal statement identifies this derivative with the alternating-symbol contraction of the Hessian.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityPosWith_se.text: The paper uses the positive density defining I⁺. The formal identity states that substituting the classical Hessian into the weak-Hessian formula recovers its classical expression pointwise.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith_se.text: The paper uses the negative density defining I⁻. The formal identity states that substituting the classical Hessian into the weak-Hessian formula recovers its classical expression pointwise.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.isAdmissibleWeak_.text: The paper presents one set of multiplier admissibility conditions. The formal statement relates the classical and weak-Hessian versions under C² regularity, using the identity for ∇curl W.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: Proposition B.1 uses c=3/50 and the described profile and weight data. The formal theorem allows general admissible coefficients and explicit weak-Hessian representatives, and writes the density inequality through separate positive and negative masses.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith_s.text: The paper uses one bound for the norm of ∇curl W. For a C² field the formal statement identifies the time-angle supremum computed from the Hessian with the supremum computed from that derivative.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsRestModeW.text: The paper uses the curl-piece interaction remainder within the multiplier estimate. The formal identity replaces the supplied weak Hessian by the classical second derivative and recovers the classical remainder formula.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsBlockWith.text: The paper estimates the curl-piece block terms in the multiplier argument. The formal identity recovers the classical block expression from its weak-Hessian version under C² regularity.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceRestWith_sec.text: The paper combines the mode remainders as part of the density estimate. The formal identity states that their weak-Hessian sum becomes the classical sum after substituting the classical Hessian.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceBlockWith_se.text: The paper uses the aggregate block remainder in the multiplier argument. Under C² regularity the formal identity recovers its classical expression from the weak-Hessian formula.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: The proof of Proposition B.1 uses multiplier existence, smooth approximation, passage to the limit and absorption of errors. The formal statement assumes these four assertions and concludes the full multiplier assertion.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: The paper includes (7.18) among the certificate conditions. The formal statement extracts that condition from a complete certificate; its proof supplies no new verification of the estimate from cell data.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rows_nonneg.text: The paper treats [F] as a seminorm on H. The formal lemma states only that the square-root formula is nonnegative, which holds even before the row and weight conditions needed for a seminorm are imposed.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.zero_mem_params.text: The paper states that K in (7.29) contains the origin. The formal statement proves exactly this for the mixed coordinate-box and scaled-ball constraint, using the signs of the separate coordinate radii.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.actuator_finite.text: The paper assumes bᵢ∈H and the aggregate bound (7.9). The formal statement extracts finiteness of each squared period integral from the finite upper bound on their sum.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: Lemma B.2 gives the a priori estimate for the printed coefficients $3/50$ and $1000$. The formal implication is uniform in the parameter and allows general $c,t$, with the explicit comparisons $a/\sqrt{c}\le c_1$ and $\sqrt{t/c}\le c_2$.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq.text: The paper combines its specialized density inequalities inside Lemma B.2. The formal implication isolates that combination for general coefficients, parameter-dependent weights and a specified weak Hessian.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: Proposition B.1 and Lemma B.2 together turn the multiplier construction and remaining density lower bound into coercivity. The formal implication keeps that lower bound and the two scalar coefficient comparisons as hypotheses, so it does not verify a particular numerical certificate.

families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).
